articles.title: 590 Bus Route from Rochdale to Halifax Showcases Scenic Pennine Journey
articles.excerpt: The 590 bus service from Rochdale to Halifax provides passengers with a picturesque view of Greater Manchester's industrial heritage and dramatic landscapes for just £2.50.
articles.content_html:
The 590 bus service from Rochdale to Halifax has been highlighted as a scenic journey across the Pennines, offering passengers a unique view of the region's industrial heritage and dramatic landscapes. The service, operated by First Bus, departs from Rochdale bus station and travels through Smallbridge and Littleborough before crossing into West Yorkshire.

As the bus ascends into the hills, passengers can enjoy sights such as the gritstone ridge of Blackstone Edge and the historic Summit Tunnel, designed by George Stephenson. This tunnel, which opened in 1841, was once the longest railway tunnel in the world and is a testament to Victorian engineering. It was also the site of a significant underground fire in 1984, which took firefighters four days to extinguish.

Along the route, the Rochdale Canal can be seen, which was opened 37 years before the Summit Tunnel and is one of the highest canals in England. The canal, once bustling with barges transporting goods, now attracts leisure activities such as kayaking and pleasure cruising. The journey also offers glimpses of local wildlife, including a herd of alpacas grazing near the canal.

The fare for a single journey on the 590 is £2.50, reflecting its status as a privately-owned service. This affordable price allows locals and visitors alike to explore the scenic beauty and historical significance of the area, making it a worthwhile experience for anyone travelling between Rochdale and Halifax.

articles.title: Construction Begins on New Logistics Unit at Birch Business Park, Heywood
articles.excerpt: A new urban logistics unit is being built at Birch Business Park in Heywood, expected to enhance local industrial operations and create jobs in the region.
articles.content_html:
Construction has commenced on a new 103,770 square foot urban logistics unit at Birch Business Park in Heywood. The facility, named Birch 100, is being developed in the south-east corner of the 15.6-hectare estate, which is strategically located next to junction 3 of the M66 and junction 19 of the M62.

The new unit is expected to support the existing industrial and logistics operations in the area. McCarthy and Stone, the anticipated tenant, plans to utilise the facility for the maintenance of heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) and cranes, as well as a fuelling point. This development is part of a broader expansion of the Birch Business Park, which aims to meet the growing demand for quality industrial space in the North West.

The project is being delivered by Chancerygate, an urban logistics developer and investment manager, who will also refurbish three additional units on the estate. Completion of Birch 100 is expected in summer 2027, contributing to the Northern Gateway initiative, a 1,600-acre employment area straddling the borders of Bury and Rochdale.

Mike Walker, head of Chancerygate’s North West office, stated that the development marks an important step for Birch Business Park, highlighting the pent-up demand for sustainable business space in the region. The Northern Gateway project is anticipated to create up to 10,000 jobs and provide 6.5 million square feet of industrial space, significantly boosting the local economy.

articles.title: Residents Raise Concerns Over Late-Night Licensing for Burger Box on Milkstone Road
articles.excerpt: Residents have expressed fears regarding a fast-food restaurant's application to extend its opening hours until 3am, citing potential increases in anti-social behaviour and noise.
articles.content_html:
Residents on Milkstone Road have raised concerns about a fast-food restaurant's application to extend its opening hours until 3am daily. The application, submitted for the Burger Box at 26 Milkstone Road, seeks to modify the current licence that permits operation from 11am to 11pm, with reduced hours on Sundays and bank holidays.

The Rochdale Council's Licensing Sub-Committee is set to review the application on Monday, October 12. The premises licence holder, Kashif Hazarbuz, has applied for the extended hours, which would allow the restaurant to operate late into the night. Currently, the restaurant is permitted to provide eat-in, collection, and delivery services during the specified hours, and no alcohol is allowed on the premises at any time.

Local residents have voiced their objections, with one resident, Mrs S Rana, expressing concerns about potential increases in anti-social behaviour and noise pollution if the licence is granted. Another resident, Mr I Hussain, echoed these sentiments, stating that the late-night operation could attract crime and create a public nuisance for those living nearby.

The outcome of the Licensing Sub-Committee's meeting will determine whether the Burger Box will be allowed to operate until 3am, which could significantly impact the local community's peace and safety. Residents are encouraged to monitor the decision and consider its implications for the area.

articles.title: New Support for Over 20,000 Carers Unveiled at Rochdale Event
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has launched new support initiatives for over 20,000 local carers during a recent event aimed at recognising their contributions.
articles.content_html:
More than 20,000 carers in the Rochdale borough were recognised for their invaluable contributions during a special event held at Rochdale Council’s offices at Number One Riverside. The Carers’ Collaborative Event, hosted by Rochdale Council Adult Social Care and the Collaboration Steering Group, unveiled new support measures designed to assist those who care for loved ones.

The event also marked the launch of the Heywood, Middleton and Rochdale Carers’ Strategy, which aims to provide comprehensive information and resources focused on the health and wellbeing of carers. Attendees had the opportunity to undergo free health checks, connect with other carers, and learn about various services available to them in the community.

Rochdale Council expressed gratitude to all those who attended and supported the event, highlighting the importance of the help and advice available to the 20,000 carers residing in Heywood, Middleton, Pennines, and Rochdale. The council shared on its Facebook page, thanking everyone involved in making the event a success.

This initiative is part of ongoing efforts to support the local caring community, ensuring that those who dedicate their time to caring for others receive the necessary assistance and recognition. Further details about the support available can be found on the Rochdale Council website.

articles.title: Rochdale Sixth Form College to Host Open Events for Prospective Students
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Sixth Form College invites prospective students and their families to attend Open Events on 17 October and 19 November, providing insights into courses and college life.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Sixth Form College is inviting prospective students and their families to its upcoming Open Events, designed to showcase the college's offerings and facilities. The events will take place on Saturday 17 October from 10am to 2pm and Thursday 19 November from 4pm to 7pm.

During the Open Day and Open Evening, visitors will have the opportunity to meet experienced tutors, speak with current Student Ambassadors, and explore the wide range of A level and vocational courses available. The college is recognised as one of the UK's leading sixth form providers, particularly noted for its value-added performance, which reflects the progress students make during their studies.

The Principal’s Talk will be held at various times throughout each event, allowing attendees to gain insights directly from the college leadership. There is no need to book a separate place for the talk; visitors are encouraged to arrive at the Theatre on the first floor approximately ten minutes before the scheduled start time. The talks are scheduled for 10:30am, 11:15am, 12pm, and 12:45pm on 17 October, and at 4:30pm, 5:15pm, and 6pm on 19 November.

To attend the Open Events, prospective students must book their places in advance. More information and booking details can be found on the college's website at www.rochdalesfc.ac.uk/open-events. All students are expected to be accompanied by a parent or carer.

articles.title: Littleborough Dancers Achieve Eight First Places at Ibiza Championships
articles.excerpt: Six dancers from Resisdance Company in Littleborough excelled at the Ibiza International Dance Championships, securing eight first places and five top-three finishes.
articles.content_html:
Six dancers from Resisdance Company in Littleborough achieved significant success at the Ibiza International Dance Championships, returning home with eight first places and five additional top-three podium finishes. The dancers, aged between 10 and 17, competed against various international participants, showcasing their talent on a global stage.

Principal Danielle Lee expressed pride in the dancers' accomplishments, noting that they made 20 finals appearances during the competition. "Overall we took six dancers and came back to the UK with 20 finals including eight winners (1st places) and five top-three podium places," she stated. "It is a remarkable achievement competing overseas!"

The Ibiza International Dance Championships provided a platform for young dancers to demonstrate their skills and dedication, with competitors from various countries participating. The event not only highlighted the talent of the Littleborough dancers but also promoted cultural exchange through dance.

This success is likely to inspire other young dancers in the local community, encouraging them to pursue their passion for dance and participate in future competitions. Resisdance Company continues to foster talent and provide opportunities for dancers to excel both locally and internationally.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky niche called the Fairies’ Chapel is real; the fairies, dwarf‑sentinel and fairy‑king belong to two centuries of storytelling rather than to the official record.
articles.summary: The rocky niche called the Fairies’ Chapel is real; the fairies, dwarf‑sentinel and fairy‑king belong to two centuries of storytelling rather than to the official record.
articles.body:
Stand by the Thrutch in Healey Dell — the narrow, fern‑clad cleft where the River Spodden tumbles beneath the 19th‑century viaduct — and it’s easy to see why imagination settled here. A water‑carved alcove in the rock has long looked like a tiny pulpit with bench‑like seats, and generations of local guides and storytellers have called that ledge the Fairies’ Chapel.

What is documented

Healey Dell is a recorded local nature reserve and visitor site managed and described by Rochdale Borough Council. The reserve contains visible industrial archaeology (mill remains), woodland, waterfalls and the dramatic Healey Dell Viaduct, which is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those are verifiable facts you can map, photograph and inspect today. The council’s visitor directory and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre provide route maps, historical notes and on‑site interpretation for visitors.

Historic sources show the chapel‑like rock formation was a named local feature by the 19th century and that the Dell’s appearance changed after a violent summer storm commonly called the “July flood” (often dated to 4 July 1838 in contemporary and later accounts). Nineteenth‑century writers and later guide material note that parts of the Fairies’ Chapel were altered or damaged by that event; some modern guides give 1839 as the year, which reflects variation in later retellings of local weather‑history. The viaduct’s listing and the reserve’s present facilities are recorded on official sites and heritage registers.

What belongs to folklore

The more colourful material — a Healey Dwarf, a Fairy Queen or King, witches turned to stone, prophetic utterances and even a local link to a Robin Hood figure — comes from folklore collections and Victorian‑era retellings rather than from administrative records. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (early 19th century) is one of the earliest printed sources to record the Fairies’ Chapel stories collected from local oral tradition; later nineteenth‑century verses and guidebooks elaborated those tales and fixed many of the characters and episodes now associated with the Dell.

Local interpretation at the Healey Dell Heritage Centre and in printed trail guides explicitly treat these elements as legend and cultural memory. They explain how the river’s erosive action could produce pulpit‑like hollows that invited romantic and supernatural readings. Where nineteenth‑century collectors recorded what people were telling, modern custodians reproduce those stories as part of the Dell’s living heritage — useful for family events and atmosphere, but not evidence of literally supernatural events.

How to read the stories

Treat the Fairies’ Chapel as a place where geology, industry and storytelling meet. The rock alcove and mill remains are tangible. The Healey Dwarf, Fairy Queen, witches‑turned‑to‑stone and the Fairy King are narrative motifs preserved in printed folklore and later guidebooks; they explain why the spot excited local imagination but they do not appear in documentary records as eyewitness or official events. If a story requires a precise historical claim (a date, a named witness, an inspection report), look for it in archival or council records; many of the supernatural details cannot be verified in that way and are best understood as tradition.

If you visit

Bring stout footwear and curiosity rather than certainty. Walk the trails, read the Heritage Centre’s interpretation panels and enjoy the mix of dramatic stone, rushing water and Victorian engineering. If you want the earliest printed flavour of the tales, read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire; if you want the site‑level history and visitor information, the Rochdale Borough Council listing and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre material set out what is documented and what is told for pleasure.

In short: the Fairies’ Chapel is real as a rock feature and a named place. The fairies, dwarf and fairy‑king live in the county’s storytelling tradition — cherished, retold and performed — but they are not supported by independent documentary evidence as literal events.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway wins Community Hero Award for its volunteers
articles.excerpt: East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.

The awards celebrate people, groups, charities and businesses that go the extra mile to support others and strengthen their communities. The railway said the recognition reflects the commitment of its volunteers and the role the heritage line continues to play across the communities it serves.

The East Lancashire Railway operates heritage trains through the Irwell Valley, connecting communities including Bury, Summerseat, Ramsbottom, Irwell Vale, Rawtenstall and Heywood.

Diesel Driver and Head of the Signalling Department Linda Henderson said the railway could not exist without its volunteers.

"For almost 40 years, the ELR has operated Heritage trains through the heart of the Irwell Valley. Without volunteers, the ELR and Heritage Railways throughout the UK would not exist."

Henderson said the award recognised more than 800 current volunteers as well as those who had previously given their time to the railway.

Chairman Mike Kelly said he was "extremely proud" to accept the award on behalf of the railway and its volunteers, describing their work as generous and unselfish.

Kelly, who is also a volunteer, said the recognition highlighted the commitment and passion volunteers bring to organisations across local communities. He also thanked Roch Valley Radio for recognising volunteers and the contribution they make to charities and community organisations.

The award was collected by a group of volunteers representing several parts of the railway, including train operations, signalling, the guards department, the dining train team and a station café.

The East Lancashire Railway said the award was a recognition of the hard work and continued dedication of all its volunteers.

articles.title: Rochdale Sleepout 2026 returns to raise funds and awareness for people facing homelessness
articles.excerpt: Petrus is calling on Rochdale residents, businesses and community groups to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026 and help raise vital funds for local people experiencing homelessness and social exclusion.
articles.content_html:
Petrus Community is calling on people across Rochdale to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026, a fundraising and awareness event designed to highlight the realities faced by people experiencing homelessness while raising vital funds for local support services.

The Rochdale-based charity supports people experiencing homelessness, poverty and social exclusion across the borough. The Sleepout challenges participants to spend a night outdoors while learning more about homelessness and the support available locally.

Organisers are keen to stress that the event is not intended to replicate the experience of homelessness. Instead, it aims to encourage conversation, build understanding and raise money to support people accessing Petrus services.

Last year's inaugural Rochdale Sleepout brought supporters together from across the borough and raised £7,875.52 for Rochdale AFC Community Trust and Petrus.

The money raised has already helped launch Changing Lives, a partnership supporting people experiencing homelessness and those living in supported accommodation through football, wellbeing, education and employability opportunities.

According to Petrus, participants involved in the programme are rebuilding confidence, making new friendships, developing new skills and becoming more active members of their communities.

This year's event is also an opportunity for local businesses, community groups and individuals to get involved by taking part, sponsoring participants or making a donation.

Funds raised through the Sleepout will support Petrus' work across Rochdale, including homelessness prevention, housing support, wellbeing services, education and training opportunities, and practical support for some of the borough's most vulnerable residents.

Petrus is encouraging anyone interested in supporting the event to help spread the word and get involved.

articles.title: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers take on 45-mile charity walk
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are taking on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October, to raise money for four causes close to their hearts.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are swapping the rugby pitch for the road as members of the groups prepare to take on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October.

The challenge is being organised to raise as much money as possible for four causes close to the participants' hearts: Springhill Hospice, the Motor Neurone Disease Association (MND), Rochdale Masters and Rugby League Cares.

Organisers are expecting the walk to be a major physical challenge, but say they want it to become about more than completing 45 miles. They are also appealing to local businesses and members of the community to get behind the fundraising effort.

Businesses are being encouraged to support the challenge through sponsorship, donations, supplies for the day or simply by sharing the fundraiser with customers, colleagues and their wider networks.

The organisers said: "We're not playing rugby for this one… we're putting the boots down and walking 45 miles!"

The group hopes that local support will help raise as much money as possible for the four causes while bringing businesses, sports communities and residents together around the challenge.

Anyone who can help with sponsorship, donations, supplies or promotion is encouraged to get in touch with the organisers.

Mandy from Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers said the group would be happy to provide photographs, route details and further information about the charities involved, as well as speak about the challenge.

articles.title: 'Rochdale's Chernobyl' to Undergo Clean-Up Ahead of Redevelopment
articles.excerpt: The former Turner Brothers asbestos factory site, known as 'Rochdale's Chernobyl', is set for a clean-up as part of plans for redevelopment, with a specialist contractor appointed to begin remediation work.
articles.content_html:
The notorious former Turner Brothers asbestos factory site in Spotland, Rochdale, is poised for a significant clean-up as part of a major redevelopment initiative. The site, often referred to as 'Rochdale's Chernobyl', has been derelict for decades and is known for its hazardous conditions due to the asbestos previously manufactured there.

Landowners Spodden Park Ltd have appointed a specialist contractor to carry out remediation work on the 75-acre site, which was once the world's largest asbestos manufacturer. The factory has remained off-limits to the public, with only a few daring 'urban explorers' venturing onto the property, which has been described as decaying and dangerous.

Local residents have long expressed a desire to see the site transformed into a community asset, with proposals ranging from housing developments to public parks. Although previous redevelopment efforts have failed, Spodden Park Ltd aims to approach the project with safety as a priority, particularly given the carcinogenic nature of the materials involved. While specific plans for the site have yet to be disclosed, it is understood that any housing development will involve far fewer units than the 650 proposed in earlier plans from the 2000s.

The clean-up marks a crucial step towards making the site viable for future development. Once the remediation is completed, the land could be repurposed for housing and green spaces, aligning with the community's vision for a safer and more accessible area. Further details on the redevelopment plans are expected to be announced following the clean-up.

articles.title: Failsworth Tram Stop Lift Out of Service During Replacement Works
articles.excerpt: The lift at Failsworth tram stop is currently out of service, affecting access for passengers. Those needing step-free access are advised to use alternative routes.
articles.content_html:
The lift at Failsworth tram stop, which services the platform heading towards Rochdale, is currently out of service due to ongoing lift replacement works. This situation has resulted in a lack of step-free access at the stop, which may affect passengers with mobility issues.

Passengers are advised to make their way to Hollinwood tram stop to connect to services during this period. The lift on the platform heading towards East Didsbury is also out of service, compounding accessibility challenges at this location.

For those requiring step-free access, it is recommended to contact the Metrolink customer service centre for assistance with journey planning. The contact number is 0161 244 1000, with lines open from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and 8am to 8pm on weekends and Bank Holidays.

The duration of the lift outage is currently unspecified, and updates will be provided as the situation develops. Passengers are encouraged to check the latest travel alerts for further information.

articles.title: Police Seize £2 Million Worth of Suspected Cocaine and Cannabis Farms in Middleton
articles.excerpt: A vehicle stop in Middleton led police to seize 20 kilograms of suspected cocaine and uncover three cannabis farms, resulting in the arrest of a 38-year-old man.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

07:01, 06 October 2026

A vehicle stop in Middleton led to the seizure of 20 kilograms of suspected cocaine and the discovery of three cannabis farms, resulting in the arrest of a 38-year-old man.

05:25, 06 October 2026

Following a vehicle stop in Middleton, police have seized 20 kilograms of suspected cocaine and uncovered three cannabis farms, leading to the arrest of a 38-year-old man.

01:55, 06 October 2026

Following a vehicle stop in Middleton on October 4, police seized 20 kilograms of suspected cocaine and uncovered three cannabis farms, leading to the arrest of a 38-year-old man.

Police in Middleton seized 20 kilograms of suspected cocaine and discovered three cannabis farms following a vehicle stop on Sunday, October 4. The operation was carried out by officers from Middleton’s Neighbourhood Policing Team, who identified a suspicious vehicle parked on Cemetery Street during their patrol.

Upon searching the vehicle, officers found a significant quantity of Class A drugs, along with scales and cash. This led to the arrest of a 38-year-old man on suspicion of possession with intent to supply Class A drugs. He remains in custody for questioning as investigations continue.

Further intelligence prompted police to search two addresses in Middleton and one in Chadderton, Oldham. At each location, officers found cannabis farms and recovered the suspected cocaine, which has an estimated street value of around £2 million.

The seized substances are currently awaiting further assessment. Greater Manchester Police have not yet released additional details regarding the arrested individual or the ongoing investigation.
